## Example 1.3 · Rewrite using base $e$ {#dc1-example-1-3-rewrite .dc-lesson}

<p>Consider the function <span data-math="y=a^x"></span> where <span data-math="a"></span> is a constant and <span data-math="a>0"></span>.</p>
<p class="dc-prompt"><strong>a)</strong> Using the identity <span data-math="a=e^{\ln a}"></span>, rewrite <span data-math="a^x"></span> as an exponential function with base <span data-math="e"></span>.</p>
<div data-dc-steps class="dc-stepper "><div aria-live="polite"><div class="dc-step" hidden><p class="dc-step-label">Replace the base with an equal expression.</p><span data-math="a^x=\left(e^{{\color{#b55224}\ln a}}\right)^x"></span></div><div class="dc-step" hidden><p class="dc-step-label">Use the power-of-a-power index law.</p><span data-math="\left(e^{{\color{#b55224}\ln a}}\right)^x=e^{x{\color{#b55224}\ln a}}"></span></div></div><div class="dc-step-controls"><button type="button" class="dc-step-back">Hide last step</button><button type="button" class="dc-step-next primary">Reveal next step</button><button type="button" class="dc-step-reset">Reset</button><span class="dc-step-count" aria-live="polite"></span></div></div><p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 3 · Example 1.3(a)</p>

::: notes
Each tap reveals one step. Ask students to predict the next line, then justify it using an inverse identity or an index law. Orange identifies the same constant ln a in every line. a>0 ensures ln a is defined. Even a=1 is allowed: it gives the constant function 1. This is an equivalent expression for the same function, not an approximation or a change of function. Follow-up: “We now have base e. What is the derivative of its exponent?” Answers remain hidden until deliberately revealed. Use Hide last step or Reset to repeat.
:::
